scenes.tts: A lumber merchant's son once written off as "too stupid to be a businessman," Fischer became the most formidable organic chemist in Germany by reading structure off behavior.
scenes.visual: portrait inset; lumber merchant son, written off, most formidable organic chemist in Germany, structure read off behavior
scenes.narration: A lumber merchant's son once written off as "too stupid to be a businessman," Fischer became the most formidable organic chemist in Germany by reading structure off behavior.

scenes.tts: The same instinct that let him cage the geometry of sugars let him see proteins clearly: at a congress in Karlsbad in September 1902 he introduced the word "peptides" and named the bond that links one amino acid to the next — the backbone of every protein you will ever study.

scenes.narration: The same instinct that let him cage the geometry of sugars let him see proteins clearly: at a congress in Karlsbad in September 1902 he introduced the word "peptides" and named the bond that links one amino acid to the next — the backbone of every protein you will ever study.

scenes.tts: (Franz Hofmeister announced the same amide-bond conclusion independently at that very congress; the name is Fischer's, the insight was in the air.) In an 1894 lecture he had already declared that chemists could now build life's active molecules "without any assistance from a living organism," three years before Buchner's cell-free extract delivered vitalism its decisive blow.

scenes.tts: The tool that made all of it possible was also killing him: phenylhydrazine, the compound he discovered in 1875 to fingerprint sugars, poisoned him slowly across decades of bench work. By 1919, with inoperable cancer almost certainly from that exposure, and two of his three sons lost in a single winter of the war, he took his own life on July 15.
